title: Once Upon a Time in Mexico
full_review:
Robert Rodriguez's enigmatic mariachi assassin returns with a guitar case full of ammo and a soul bent on revenge in "Once Upon a Time in Mexico" (Columbia).

This third and final chapter in Rodriguez's "Mariachi Trilogy" adds nothing new to the visually stylish -- but gratuitously violent -- franchise except for yet another ridiculously high body count -- and, as the mythic title suggests, a more epic stage for its ballistic bloodbath.

Strumming and gunning his way through the carnage like a matador with an Uzi is Antonio Banderas as the nameless guitar-slinger who, as the curtain rises, has withdrawn into a life of pacifism, haunted by the death of his wife, Carolina (Salma Hayek), and child. Both, as told through flashbacks, were killed by the villainous Marquez (Gerardo Vigil), generalissimo of a guerrilla junta and Carolina's jealous former lover.

Without much arm-twisting, the reclusive hero is lured out of retirement by a rogue CIA spook (Johnny Depp), who extorts El Mariachi into sabotaging the plot of a notorious cartel kingpin, Barillo (Willem Dafoe), to assassinate the president of Mexico.
Forswearing his short-lived, turn-the-other-cheek vow, El Mariachi complies, secretly biding his time in order to exact his revenge on Marquez, who is in cahoots with Barillo. The drug czar orders the general's forces to stage a coup d'etat against the president, an uprising which forms the backdrop of the flick's over-the-top, bloody and bullet-ridden finale between Marquez and El Mariachi -- who has enlisted the aid of two fellow pistoleros (Enrique Iglesias and Marco Leonardi).

All this sounds much more confusing than it really is, since the skeletal vengeance-driven premise is merely a perfunctory device on which to hang the slickly choreographed shoot-'em ups -- including a flamenco-rhythm gun battle offensively set in a church -- that supply the narrative's real impetus.

Filmmaker Rodriguez launched his career in 1992 with the shoestring-budgeted "El Mariachi," continuing the sanguinary saga in 2001 with his amped-up half-sequel, half-remake "Desperado." All three movies borrow heavily from Sergio Leone's spaghetti westerns, combining B-movie conventions with a high-octane, self-conscious style and wickedly dark humor.

Throughout the film, Rodriguez juxtaposes violent images with religious iconography or gestures. In one scene El Mariachi makes the sign of the cross before blowing someone away. Unlike the classic baptism sequence in "The Godfather," which was used to illustrate the blasphemous hypocrisy of the Mafia dons, the irreverence of Rodriguez's film not only serves no narrative purpose, but it displays a desecrating disregard for sacred sensibilities.

Equally troubling, the movie's pervasive violence, at times so unrealistic it could be viewed as campy satire, promotes, however unintended, a skewed sense of cheapness and triviality concerning human life, treating peripheral characters as so many moving targets, to be mowed down indiscriminately -- a message which runs counter to what the film's brooding hero purportedly stands for.

Borrowing a clever play on words from Depp's scene-stealing performance, despite its flashy visual flair and sumptuous color palette, "Once Upon a Time in Mexico" is one flick that "Mexi-can't" be recommended.

Due to excessive gory violence, including profanely using a church as the setting for gunplay, brief partial frontal nudity and much rough language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
